solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Classics, to him, may be represented by such philosophical method

indicators.note: the letters of the first three words may be represented in a new order, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written: thirteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A classicist is said to be devoted to a particular old philosophical approach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be represented' tells you the letters of 'Classics, to him' are rearranged; they use every letter exactly once, and 'such' ties the definition back to the man in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Scholasticism was the medieval schoolmen's method of reasoning, built on Aristotle and Church doctrine.

clue.text: Second oldster in Gretna Green landmark?

parts.note: Chambers gives oldster as a midshipman of four years' standing, and a middy is a midshipman

explanation.surface: An elderly person turns up again at the famous Scottish wedding village.
explanation.walkthrough: Oldster here is the naval sense, a senior midshipman, not simply an old person. Runaway couples were married over the anvil at the blacksmith's shop in Gretna Green, Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: A smiddy is the Scots word for a smithy, and the blacksmith's shop is Gretna Green's best-known building.

clue.text: Artery cuts turn out red

indicators.note: the motorway cuts into the middle of the verb, so it goes inside

parts.note: to turn out, as in turn up at an event, is to come
the M1 is Britain's main north-south motorway, an arterial road, written here MI

explanation.surface: A medical note: severing an artery makes things turn out bloody red.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Artery' looks medical but is a major road, the M1 motorway in Britain, and 'cuts' puts it into the middle of COME.
explanation.definitionFit: Commie and red are both informal words for a communist.

clue.text: Plant fruit and veg on top of stone — odd

indicators.note: in a down answer, the first pieces sit above the next

parts.note: a hip is the fruit of the rose
a pea is a vegetable
ST is the abbreviation for stone, the British unit of weight
rum means odd or strange

explanation.surface: An instruction to plant fruit and vegetables on a stone base, which seems an odd idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on top of' places the fruit and veg above the stone in this down answer. A stone is 14 pounds in British weight, abbreviated ST.
explanation.definitionFit: Hippeastrum is a genus of bulbous flowering plants, sold as amaryllis.

clue.text: Office lot going wild in old dance

parts.note: Chambers gives office as a euphemism for a lavatory, shortened to lav

indicators.note: the letters of lot go wild, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The whole office staff runs riot at a period dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Office' looks like a workplace but is the old euphemism for a toilet, informally a lav; 'going wild' turns LOT into OLT.
explanation.definitionFit: The lavolt or lavolta was a lively leaping dance of the sixteenth century.

clue.text: Disappointed parishioner may find this accommodation with shared facilities (11, two words)

definitions.meaning: a churchgoer let down by worship might find the church ..., dull
a rented flat whose cleaning and other domestic services are provided

explanation.walkthrough: The first reading splits the answer into two words: a service, as in church, that is flat, as in lifeless.
explanation.definitionFit: A service flat is an apartment let with cleaning, laundry and similar services included in the rent.

clue.text: Profits turn out fine, as of old

definitions.meaning: in law, ... are the profits or produce of land
fine meaning end, as in the archaic phrase in fine

explanation.walkthrough: Three separate senses of one word sit side by side; the surface reads like a business forecast.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers yields from property, to result in some way, and in older use a conclusion.

clue.text: Questioner on the spot disheartened the conceited, first off

parts.note: being in a place is being on the spot, giving IN

indicators.note: the word the loses its heart, its middle letter

parts.note: taken as written before its middle goes

indicators.note: the first letter of the synonym is removed

parts.note: arrogant means conceited

explanation.surface: An interrogator on the scene gets the arrogant ones to lose heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disheartened' takes the H from THE, leaving TE; 'first off' drops the A of ARROGANT, leaving RROGANT.
explanation.definitionFit: An interrogant is one who interrogates, someone asking questions.

clue.text: Such Capone always retained — 'capo di tutti …'

definitions.text: Such Capone always retained — 'capo di tutti …'

indicators.note: capo is Italian for head, so the heads of all the words are taken: their first letters

parts.note: the words whose first letters are taken

explanation.surface: Al Capone, the Mafia 'boss of all bosses', bore one mark for life.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue quotes 'capo di tutti capi', boss of all bosses, but stops short: read literally, 'capo di tutti' says head of all, the first letters of 'Such Capone always retained'.
explanation.definitionFit: Al Capone was nicknamed Scarface for the facial wound he carried from a knife fight.

clue.text: The writer penning dig nastily — one may generate gall

indicators.note: the writer's word encloses the rearranged letters, as a pen encloses animals

parts.note: the writer of the clue refers to himself as me

indicators.note: the letters of dig are treated nastily, rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An author writes a spiteful dig, and the remark galls its target.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nastily' mixes the dig into IDG, which 'penning' encloses in the writer's word. 'gall' looks like resentment but is a plant growth caused by gall midges.
explanation.definitionFit: A gall midge is a tiny fly whose larvae cause abnormal swellings on plants.

clue.text: Master what's extracted from well, getting wet no longer

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for master, as in MA
oil is drawn from an oil well

explanation.surface: An expert in drilling shows how what came out of the well stops being wet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wet no longer' means a sense now obsolete, not something dried out.
explanation.definitionFit: Moil originally meant to make or become wet and muddy, a sense Chambers marks obsolete.

clue.text: Conclude subject? Not able

indicators.note: the word able is not there, so it is taken away

parts.note: amenable means subject or liable, as in amenable to the law
the letters removed

explanation.surface: A grammar question: can we wrap up the subject, or are we unable?
explanation.definitionFit: To amen something is to say the closing word to it, bringing a prayer or matter to its end.

clue.text: Fair but shunned by company, dejected within, getting rather drunk?

indicators.note: the word for dejected goes inside what is left
the company abbreviation stays away from the word, so it is removed

parts.note: comely means fair, good-looking
low means dejected

explanation.surface: A good-looking person shunned by friends and feeling low takes to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shunned by' takes the company out of the word for fair, leaving MELY, and 'within' sets LOW inside it. The question mark flags a playful extension of mellow.
explanation.definitionFit: Mellow is a mild word for slightly tipsy, and mellowy is Chambers's informal variant.

clue.text: Musician revises aims with these crotchets?

indicators.note: the musician's letters are revised, rearranged, after aims is taken out

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written
the letters taken out of the fodder

explanation.surface: A musician reworks a score and asks whether these are the right quarter notes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revises' rearranges MUSICIAN, which holds the letters of AIMS plus the answer's. 'crotchets' is not the musical note here but its older sense, hooks.
explanation.definitionFit: Unci, plural of uncus, are hooks or hooked parts, and a crotchet is also a small hook.

clue.text: Bankrupt making mischief about surplus

indicators.note: the mischief word goes about, around, the surplus word

parts.note: impish means mischievous, given to making mischief
over means surplus, as in left over

explanation.surface: A bankrupt causing trouble over the excess funds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps the mischief word around the surplus one. 'Bankrupt' is a verb here, to ruin financially.
explanation.definitionFit: To impoverish someone is to make them poor, to reduce them to ruin.

clue.text: Accumulate/fund

definitions.meaning: to ... resources is to gather them together
a ... is a common fund, as in a betting ...

explanation.walkthrough: The slash simply separates two meanings of one word, verb and noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both to combine resources and a shared kitty of money.

clue.text: Slalom's beginning at a higher place, bit of work for ski event (6, two words)

indicators.note: the beginning of the word slalom is its first letter

parts.note: the word whose first letter is taken
up means at a higher place
an erg is a small unit of work in physics

explanation.surface: A skier starts the slalom up high and puts in some effort.
explanation.definitionFit: The super-G, short for super giant slalom, is an Alpine skiing race between downhill and giant slalom.

clue.text: 'Losing weight': lines in lots of printing matter read up

indicators.note: the lines go inside the reversed word
in a down answer the word is read upwards, from bottom to top

parts.note: reams are large quantities of paper for printing

explanation.surface: A slimming headline, with lines set into piles of printed matter for revision.
explanation.walkthrough: Reams are packs of 500 sheets of paper, so lots of printing matter; 'read up' reverses them to SMAER in this down answer and 'in' places the lines inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone losing weight is getting smaller, shrinking in size.

clue.text: Regular intake to merge with Eton's second

parts.note: to die into something, as colours do, is to fade and merge

indicators.note: the second letter of Eton is taken

parts.note: the word whose second letter is used

explanation.surface: A school's annual intake merges with Eton's second cohort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'second' picks the T of Eton. 'intake' suggests new pupils at Eton College, the English public school, but it is food.
explanation.definitionFit: A diet is the food a person habitually eats, their usual consumption.

clue.text: Poetry has to be still around in Der Lindenbaum (8, two words)

indicators.note: the word for being still goes around the poetry word

parts.note: to lie is to be still, at rest
metre is the measured rhythm of verse, poetry

explanation.surface: Verse must be quiet around a famous Schubert song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' wraps the word for being still about the poetry word. 'Der Lindenbaum' is a song from Schubert's Winterreise; in German the title names a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: Der Lindenbaum is German for the linden, the tree British English calls a lime.

clue.text: Old head still taking in all sections

indicators.note: the word for still takes the other piece into its middle

parts.note: yet means still, as in not yet over
A is an abbreviation for all, as in the A certificate
S is the abbreviation for section, doubled here as plural

explanation.surface: A long-serving head teacher still taking in every class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking in' puts the abbreviations A and S inside YET. 'head' is not a person but the froth on a liquid, and 'Old' marks the sense as archaic.
explanation.definitionFit: Yeast once meant foam or froth, the frothy top on beer, a sense Chambers gives as obsolete.

clue.text: Policeman, for some a bit of a sugar daddy

indicators.note: only a bit of the phrase, part of its letters running across the two words, is used

parts.note: the words that hold the answer

explanation.surface: A police officer, it seems, is a kind of sugar daddy to some.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a bit of' points to letters inside 'sugar daddy'. 'for some' says the word is used only by some people, here the Irish.
explanation.definitionFit: The Garda is the Irish police force, and a garda is one of its officers.

clue.text: Early flight large birds must get about right

indicators.note: the birds go about, around, the letter for right

parts.note: geese are large birds

explanation.surface: Large birds take to the air early in the morning and circle right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'must get about' puts GEESE around R. 'flight' suggests birds in the air but means stairs; 'Early' marks an old word.
explanation.definitionFit: Greese is an old word for a flight of steps, a staircase.

clue.text: Fruitcake compounded fat blocking sink

indicators.note: the mixed letters block the sink word by sitting in it

parts.note: to die away is to sink, to decline

indicators.note: the letters of fat are compounded, mixed up

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A kitchen mishap: a fatty compound blocking the sink, as in a fruitcake recipe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'compounded' mixes the fat into AFT, and 'blocking' lodges it in the sink word. 'Fruitcake' looks like baking but is slang for an oddball.
explanation.definitionFit: A fruitcake is slang for an eccentric or crazy person, and a daftie is a silly one.

clue.text: Name held by a dignitary pertaining to chain

indicators.note: the letter for name is held inside the other pieces

parts.note: a dean is a church or university dignitary

explanation.surface: A dignitary's name connected to a chain of office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'held by' puts N inside A DEAN. 'chain' suggests a mayor's chain of office but means a mountain range.
explanation.definitionFit: Andean describes the Andes, the great mountain range or chain of South America.

clue.text: Draw bowl deployed with side

indicators.note: the letters are deployed, set out in a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cricket captain bowls a side to a draw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deployed' rearranges BOWL and SIDE. 'Draw' looks like a tied match but is the old verb meaning to disembowel, as in hanged, drawn and quartered.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw a carcass or a condemned man is to remove the entrails, to disembowel.

clue.text: Herd on the move split after opening of defile

indicators.note: the split word comes after the letter
the opening of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the word whose first letter is taken
a rift is a split

explanation.surface: Cattle on the move break up after entering a narrow mountain pass.
explanation.definitionFit: A drift is a drove of cattle or sheep being moved along.

clue.text: Sermonize: 'Some petar (own) will be hoisted'

indicators.note: in a down answer, hoisting the letters raises them, reading them bottom to top
only some of the letters, running across the two words, are taken

parts.note: the words holding the answer

explanation.surface: A preacher quotes Hamlet: the engineer will be hoist with his own petard.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface echoes Hamlet's 'hoist with his own petar', a petar being a small bomb. 'Some' takes ETARO from 'petar own', and 'will be hoisted' reads it upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To orate is to speak pompously, to deliver a sermon-like speech.

clue.text: Unanswerable question, something that floors you if old

parts.note: a KO, a knockout, puts a boxer on the floor
an is an archaic word for if

explanation.surface: A baffling question would knock you down, in the old days.
explanation.definitionFit: A koan is a Zen Buddhist riddle with no logical answer, used to provoke insight.

clue.text: King's seal denoting club

parts.note: R is short for Rex, Latin for king
an otary is an eared seal, such as a sea lion

explanation.surface: A monarch's seal on a document marks membership of a club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seal' looks like a royal stamp but is the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotary describes Rotary International, the service club whose local branches are Rotary clubs.

clue.text: Kind of arch, I'll be put up over either side of entrance

indicators.note: in a down answer, the reversed word sits over the next letter
in a down answer, the word is put up, read from the bottom

parts.note: the ego is the I, the self

indicators.note: either outside letter of entrance is the same letter, so one of them is taken

parts.note: the word whose outside letter is used

explanation.surface: A builder promises to put up an arch over an entrance.
explanation.walkthrough: I'll is read as I = EGO; 'be put up' reverses it to OGE, and 'over' sets that above 'either side of entrance', which is E whichever end you take.
explanation.definitionFit: An ogee arch has two S-shaped curves meeting in a point at its apex.

clue.text: The old tarry tucking into full English

indicators.note: the answer is tucked into the two words, spanning them

parts.note: the words holding the answer

explanation.surface: An old man lingers, tucking into a full English breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: A full English is a cooked British breakfast of bacon, eggs and sausages; 'tucking into' looks like eating.
explanation.definitionFit: Leng is an obsolete verb meaning to linger or stay, the old equivalent of tarry.

clue.text: Rickety wicket, say, needing hammer all round (10, two words)

indicators.note: the hammer word goes all round the other piece

parts.note: to malleate is to hammer metal thin
EG, for example, is what say often means

explanation.surface: A cricket groundsman needs a mallet to sort out a crumbling wicket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all round' puts the verb for hammer around the abbreviation for say. 'wicket' looks like cricket but is a small gate; 'needing' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: A mallee gate is an Australian makeshift gate built from mallee scrub, hence rickety.

clue.text: Trouble and strife directly following from behind

indicators.note: the pieces are read from behind, last letter first

parts.note: due means directly, as in due north
F is the abbreviation for following, as in page references

explanation.surface: A wife, in rhyming slang, follows right behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from behind' reads DUE and F backwards. 'Trouble and strife' is Cockney rhyming slang for wife, but here it means literally trouble and conflict.
explanation.definitionFit: A feud is a prolonged quarrel, bitter conflict between parties.

clue.text: Top French army officer Hal dispatched in war

indicators.note: Hal is dispatched, sent off, removed from the word

parts.note: a marshal, maréchal de France, is the highest French army rank
the letters removed

explanation.surface: A French marshal sends Prince Hal off to fight, as in Shakespeare's Henry V.
explanation.definitionFit: Mars, the Roman god of war, stands by metonymy for war itself.

clue.text: Cranial eminences visible in brainiacs?

indicators.note: the answer is visible inside the letters of the word

parts.note: the word holding the answer

explanation.surface: Do clever people's skulls have noticeable bumps?
explanation.definitionFit: Inia, plural of inion, are the bony protuberances at the back of the skull.

clue.text: Lovely spot, US island — live protected, once battered by storms

parts.note: Tempe is the beautiful valley in Thessaly, used for any lovely valley

indicators.note: the word for live is protected inside the island

parts.note: Staten Island is part of New York City
to be is to live, exist

explanation.surface: A beautiful US island where people live safely, though storms once hammered it.
explanation.walkthrough: Tempe is the Vale of Tempe in Greece, a byword for beauty; 'protected' shelters the word for live inside the New York island, giving STBEATEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Tempest-beaten is an old poetic adjective for something lashed by violent weather.
